title: Server-side, deny-by-default, centrally enforced authorization
status_rationale: SEC-AUTH-001 (proposed) requires deny by default and explicit server-side authorization with central enforcement and negative tests. CNV-GOV-010 requires every API command to declare its class and commands absent from the authority matrix to be refused. CNV-PLT-010 requires authorization decisions to be computed or re-verified on the server inside the command transaction and API contracts not to accept client-computed results. UNB-TEN-003 extends deny-by-default to administrator, background job, support, analytics and agent paths. Nothing is implemented.
target_answer: All Unbound capabilities are reachable only through governed F# command and query handlers. A handler cannot be registered without declaring its command class in the authority matrix; the build fails if a handler lacks a classification, and the runtime refuses unclassified commands with UnclassifiedCommand. The handler signature requires an authorization proof value that only the central authorization module can construct, so an unauthorized call path does not type-check. Decisions are evaluated server-side in the same transaction as the state change; browser-side logic in the Limen engine is display-only. Background jobs, exports, analytics, support tools and agents use the same handlers and the same proof requirement; there is no privileged side door other than break-glass.
current_practice: Not implemented. The tenant-aware persistence design contains illustrative F# contracts with private constructors that are explicitly marked not compiled (unbound@9b38de47:architecture/TENANT-AWARE-PERSISTENCE-DESIGN.md).
intended_practice: Implement the authorization core and handler registration so that missing classification fails the build and missing proof fails compilation; keep negative tests as a second line.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design enforces authorization on the server for every command, denies anything without an explicit rule, and is intended to make unauthorized call paths fail to compile. This is designed, not built or tested.
owner: Unassigned; proposed Engineering Lead with Security Lead
residual_risks: Type-level guarantees in .NET can be bypassed by reflection, unchecked casts or unsafe code unless those are also prohibited and checked (SEC-EXEC-001, SEC-LANG-001).
Correct enforcement of a wrong rule is still a vulnerability; the matrix content needs review.

challenge.customer_intent: Be certain no request can reach data or actions it is not entitled to, including through forgotten endpoints.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Missing or inconsistent authorization (OWASP A01, CWE-862, CWE-863) exposes data or enables fraud.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Conventional assurance is code review plus periodic penetration testing; both sample the surface and miss endpoints added between tests.
challenge.legally_required: No statute prescribes the technique; GLBA safeguards and interagency guidelines require access controls appropriate to risk.
challenge.contractually_required: Customers commonly require an annual third-party penetration test including authorization testing.
challenge.historical_convention: Per-endpoint checks or framework attributes, verified by penetration test.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Missing-authorization defects can be eliminated in scope: if every handler must receive a proof value constructible only by the authorization module, and every handler must be classified to be registered, a handler without authorization cannot be built. Scope excludes code that bypasses the type system (reflection, unsafe), migrations and break-glass.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Compiler and build gate; runtime refusal of unclassified commands.
challenge.continuous_evidence: The authority matrix and the handler registry can be generated from the build and compared on every release.
challenge.stronger_alternative: By-construction enforcement plus generated authorization matrix plus negative tests plus periodic independent testing focused on rule correctness and bypass of the construction.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Partially. A reviewer can inspect the proof type and registry code and run the bypass checks, but must trust the build provenance that the deployed binary came from that source.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: A bank CISO is likely to view this as strong design evidence and a reason for confidence, but unlikely to accept it in place of an independent penetration test, because examiners and the Interagency TPRM guidance expect independent verification and few bank reviewers can evaluate F# type-level arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Reflection or dynamic invocation permitted; any handler registered outside the registry; any data access not through the handlers (for example reporting queries directly on the database).
challenge.conventional_cost: Annual penetration test fees and remediation cycles.
challenge.alternative_cost: Upfront architecture effort; penetration tests still needed but can focus on rule correctness.
challenge.alternative_risks: Overconfidence: a guarantee about missing checks says nothing about incorrect checks (CWE-863).
supporting_arguments: Eliminates the most common class (missing check) rather than sampling for it.
opposing_arguments: Not yet built; the claim is architectural intent.
Type guarantees are only as strong as the prohibition of reflection and unsafe code.
Banks are institutionally required to obtain independent testing.

title: Object-level and property-level authorization (BOLA, IDOR, mass assignment)
status_rationale: RR-UNB-TEN-004-r1 AC-1 specifies RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND for out-of-scope fund requests with a denial event. UNB-PART-004 records scope for each relationship. SEC-DATA-001 requires explicit schemas at trust boundaries. Not implemented.
target_answer: Queries are constructed only through the persistence layer, which requires a VerifiedTenantContext and the principal's relationship scope; a query function that returns funds, grants or parties takes the scope as a parameter and filters at the database, so code cannot ask for 'fund 123' without asking 'fund 123 as visible to this principal'. Out-of-scope identifiers return not-found, not forbidden, and record a denial event. Commands accept explicit, versioned input schemas per role (no binding of arbitrary fields), and responses are projected per role so non-permitted fields never leave the server. Function-level authorization (what the principal may do) and object-level authorization (to which object) are both required. Identifiers may be unguessable but security never depends on that.
current_practice: Not implemented. Design and requirement text only.
intended_practice: Implement scope-parameterized query functions and role-projected responses; add negative tests per endpoint.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design checks every record request against the requester's specific relationship to that record, returns not-found for anything out of scope, and only accepts and returns fields permitted for the requester's role. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Strata does not provide a runtime typed query interface (current-state brief); the scope-parameterized data access layer must be built separately and its bypass prevented.
open_questions: Which component provides the typed, scope-parameterized query interface that SEC-DB-001 assumes, given Strata is schema management only?

challenge.customer_intent: Make sure one donor or advisor can never see or change another's fund by altering an identifier.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Broken object-level authorization (API1:2023), the most common API vulnerability class, exposes other customers' data.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Dynamic scanning rarely finds BOLA; manual penetration testing finds it when testers have two accounts and time; per-endpoint checks are easy to forget.
challenge.legally_required: No; it is an implementation of general safeguards obligations.
challenge.contractually_required: Usually covered by a penetration test requirement.
challenge.historical_convention: Per-handler ownership checks verified by pen test.
challenge.architectural_elimination: If the only way to load an object takes the principal scope as a required argument and filters in the query, the 'forgot to check ownership' defect is eliminated in scope. Scope excludes administrative tooling, reporting and any raw SQL path.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Type signatures plus database-level filtering; denial events on out-of-scope identifiers.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Denial events and property tests that generate random principal and object pairs and assert visibility equals the relationship graph.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Scope-required data access plus property-based tests over the relationship graph plus targeted independent testing.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes for the tests; partially for the type argument.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely as a strengthening; unlikely as a replacement for independent testing.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Any query path that does not require scope; caching layers that serve objects without re-checking scope.
challenge.alternative_cost: Moderate engineering in the data access layer.
challenge.alternative_risks: Scope computation itself (the relationship graph) can be wrong.
supporting_arguments: Moves the check from every call site to one mandatory parameter.
opposing_arguments: The enabling data access component does not yet exist.
Relationship-graph errors are not caught by the type system.

title: Authorization model: roles, attributes, entitlements and policy versioning
status_rationale: CNV-GOV-010 requires a single AuthorityMatrix; GOV-AUTH-008 requires checks against policy version, authority limits, effective dates, fund restrictions, liquidity and regulatory blocks; UNB-XIN-SAS-001 requires versioned, effective-dated capability entitlements enforced by authorization; GOV-AUTH-012 requires tamper-evident logging of authority decisions. Not implemented.
target_answer: Authorization combines role (what kind of actor), relationship (which funds, programs, partners), entitlement (what the customer contracted for), and context (policy version, effective dates, fund restrictions, jurisdiction, regulatory blocks) in one deterministic policy evaluated by the authorization core. Customers may compose custom roles only from permissions the platform marks delegable; reserved permissions cannot be included. Policies and entitlements are versioned, effective-dated, append-only records; each decision records the policy and entitlement versions used, so any past decision can be reproduced and explained.
intended_practice: Implement the AuthorityMatrix, entitlement records and decision logging.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design uses one deterministic authorization policy combining role, relationship, contracted entitlement and context, with every decision recording the policy version used so it can be reproduced later. This is designed, not built.
owner: Unassigned; proposed Product Owner with Security Lead
residual_risks: Model complexity can make the effective permissions hard for customers to reason about.

title: Separation of duties enforced at transaction time
status_rationale: GOV-AUTH-004 applies SoD across humans, service accounts and agents; CNV-GOV-003 requires engine-enforced SoD, a three-distinct-person rule until a deterministic release gate is accepted by the external auditor and board, reconciliation outside the payment chain, and prohibits approvers from having authoring, publishing, deployment or administration rights over the gate; CNV-GOV-005 makes author self-approval of policy changes impossible. Not implemented.
target_answer: Separation of duties is a constraint evaluated by the authorization core on every consequential command: the system refuses an approval by any principal who initiated, prepared, authored the governing policy, or has deployment or administration rights over the release gate for that transaction, and it applies across human, service and agent principals including through delegation chains. Until the sponsor's external auditor and board accept a deterministic release gate as the releaser, three distinct persons are required. Reconciliation is performed by a party outside the payment chain. Small sponsors without enough staff receive documented alternative controls with expiry and committee review, never a silent waiver.
intended_practice: Implement SoD constraints in the authority engine with delegation-chain awareness.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design has the system itself refuse any approval by someone who initiated, prepared or controls the approval policy for that transaction, across people, services and AI agents. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Collusion between distinct principals is not prevented by SoD; TVR-SEC-006 proposes detective analytics.
Sock-puppet principals for one human defeat SoD unless identity proofing links them.

challenge.customer_intent: Prevent one person from both creating and approving a fraudulent payment, and satisfy auditors that SoD is effective.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Embezzlement or error passes unchecked through a single actor.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Conventional SoD is enforced by role design reviewed periodically; conflicts are often found after the fact and do not account for delegation or agents.
challenge.legally_required: Not prescribed by statute for DAF sponsors; ICFR expectations apply to sponsors with audited financials, and SOX 404 applies only to public-company customers.
challenge.contractually_required: Sponsor auditors (SOC 1 relevance) will test SoD.
challenge.historical_convention: Maker-checker roles, periodic SoD conflict review.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Same-actor approval is eliminated in scope by transaction-time constraints that consider the full delegation chain.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Every approval records initiator, approver, chain and the SoD rule version evaluated.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Transaction-time SoD plus deterministic release gate, once the auditor accepts it.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, by negative tests (AUTH-T06, CNV-GOV-003 AC-1) and by inspecting approval records.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Transaction-time SoD is likely accepted; counting a deterministic gate as the releaser is uncertain and explicitly gated on the external auditor's acceptance.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If administrators can alter the gate policy and approve under it, or if one human controls multiple principals.
challenge.alternative_risks: A defect in the gate becomes systemic across sponsors.
supporting_arguments: Covers agents and delegations, which role review does not.
opposing_arguments: Auditor acceptance of automated releaser is uncertain.
Small sponsors may be unable to staff three distinct persons.

title: Delegated authority: scope, expiry, revocation propagation and emergency authority
status_rationale: GOV-AUTH-015 requires expiring, revocable delegation with immediate propagation; AUTH-I1 requires derived privileges to be invalidated or rechecked with a stated maximum staleness; AUTH-I2 ends child delegations with the parent; GOV-AUTH-005 requires dual control, quorum, recusal, substitute approvers and emergency authority with post-event review; CNV-GOV-008 requires every delegation to carry an expiry no later than 12 months. Not implemented.
target_answer: Delegations are first-class records naming grantor, grantee, scope (command classes, funds, limits), start, mandatory expiry and source authority; a grantor can delegate only a subset of what they hold. Ending a parent authority ends all derived delegations at the same effective time. Authority changes take effect at command execution: cached decisions, widget instances, partner tokens and agent grants derived from old authority are invalidated or rechecked on next use, within a stated maximum staleness. Changing who can approve requires dual control and cannot be self-approved. Emergency and substitute authority are pre-defined by the sponsor, time-bound and reviewed after use.
intended_practice: Implement delegation records and revocation propagation in the authorization core.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design requires every delegation to be limited, expiring and revocable, ends derived delegations with their parent, and applies authority changes to the next command. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Distributed caches and third-party registers (bank portals) may lag; AUTH-I6 brings them into scope with a revocation SLA.

title: DAF role semantics: sponsor authority versus donor, advisor and partner permissions
status_rationale: The Sponsor Authority document states donors and advisors recommend and do not gain authority to trade, approve grants or move funds; GOV-AUTH-002 separates recommendation, approval, accounting, instruction and execution; UNB-PART-003, UNB-PART-004 and UNB-PART-005 define independently assignable relationships with scope and conflict resolution; UNB-TEN-010 prevents partner preferences overriding sponsor reserved authority; UNB-AGT-002 limits agents to propose, flag, draft or open cases. Not implemented.
target_answer: The permission model encodes DAF legal structure: donor and advisor relationships (original, additional, successor, authorized viewer, professional advisor) can only create recommendations within their fund scope; approval, payment instruction and execution are sponsor-reserved command classes that no donor, advisor, partner or agent role can hold. Professional advisors see only funds where they hold a relationship. Distribution-partner staff can service their own channel's donors within sponsor-authorized data and cannot approve grants or change sponsor policy. Sponsor staff access to donor personal data is limited by role need. Concurrent recommendations and conflicts follow sponsor policy. Agents acting for donors may draft recommendations under the donor's delegation but can never approve.
intended_practice: Encode relationship types and sponsor-reserved classes in the AuthorityMatrix; test with negative cases per role.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design lets donors and advisors only recommend, reserves approval and payment decisions to the sponsor, limits partners and professional advisors to their own clients, and never allows an AI agent to approve. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Sponsor configuration may grant broad internal access; least privilege inside the sponsor depends on the sponsor's role choices (complementary user entity control).
open_questions: Counsel to confirm whether platform enforcement of recommend-only donor rights is relevant to the sponsor's exclusive legal control under IRC 4966 and the 2023 proposed regulations, or purely a product choice.

title: Authorization verification: negative tests, generated matrix and independent testing
status_rationale: SEC-AUTH-001 requires negative tests; AUTH-T01..T12 and AUTH-T05 specify authority tests; SOC2-016 requires penetration testing records; SOC2-012 requires monitoring of authorization failures. No tests exist and no independent test has occurred.
target_answer: Every command class has generated negative tests (each role attempting each command it must not perform, each principal requesting objects outside its scope) and property-based tests over random principals and objects; these run on every change and block release on failure. The effective authorization matrix is generated from the build and published to customers under NDA, with a diff per release. Production authorization denials are monitored for anomalies. An independent penetration test with authorization and tenant-isolation focus is performed before production and at least annually, with results summarized for customers.
current_practice: Nothing exists. No penetration test has been performed (current-state brief).
intended_practice: Build the negative test generator alongside the authorization core; commission an independent test before production.
customer_statement: Echelon has not yet built or independently tested Unbound's authorization. Generated negative tests on every change and an independent penetration test before production are planned.
residual_risks: Generated tests derive from the same matrix as the implementation, so they cannot detect a wrong rule; independent testing is needed for rule correctness.

challenge.customer_intent: Have confidence, backed by someone other than the vendor, that authorization cannot be bypassed.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Authorization flaws reach production and are exploited.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Annual penetration tests are time-boxed samples; findings depend on tester skill and scope; code changes after the test are untested.
challenge.legally_required: No statute requires a vendor pen test; FFIEC and interagency guidance expect banks to obtain assurance on critical vendors' controls, commonly through independent testing.
challenge.contractually_required: Very common in bank and enterprise contracts.
challenge.historical_convention: Annual third-party penetration test with summary letter.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Not applicable to the verification itself.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Negative and property tests block release.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Per-release generated matrix, test results and denial telemetry.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Continuous generated negative and property tests plus a generated matrix, with independent testing redirected at rule correctness and construction bypass.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes for test execution evidence; independent review needed to trust that tests are meaningful.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unlikely to replace the independent penetration test for banks; likely to be valued as additional evidence.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If tests are generated from the implementation rather than from an independently reviewed specification.
challenge.alternative_cost: Engineering to build the generator; penetration test still required.
challenge.alternative_risks: Circular verification if tests and code share the same mistaken model.
supporting_arguments: Every release is tested, not one snapshot per year.
opposing_arguments: Independent testing is an institutional requirement that internal tests cannot satisfy.
Generated tests share the specification's blind spots.

title: AI agent authorization boundaries
status_rationale: The Sponsor Authority document defines tiers A0 to A5 with A4 reserved for humans and A5 prohibited; UNB-RCN-PLT-005 and CNV-GOV-010 require one authority matrix by actor type; UNB-AGT-003 requires the tool broker to remove prohibited tools; UNB-AI-STD-001 requires agents to use the same governed APIs and tenant-scoped authorization as humans; UNB-RCN-PLT-004 requires agent context retrieval under the initiating principal's VerifiedTenantContext; AIN-012 requires prompt injection isolation. Not implemented.
target_answer: An agent's effective authority is the intersection of its own agent role (tier ceiling from the authority matrix) and the delegating principal's authority; it can never exceed either. Agents call the same governed command handlers as humans; the tool broker exposes only tools whose command classes are within that intersection, and the authorization core re-checks every call. Content an agent reads (charity documents, emails, web pages) is treated as untrusted data: it cannot add tools, raise tier or change targets, and consequential actions proposed after processing untrusted content require human confirmation of the exact action. Reserved (A4) and prohibited (A5) actions, including grant approval, live payments, disabling logs and changing authority, are unavailable to any agent configuration.
intended_practice: Implement agent role ceilings, intersection semantics and the tool broker.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design limits each AI agent to the overlap of its own role and the delegating user's authority, enforced by the platform on every call, and permanently withholds approval, payment and authority-changing actions from agents. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Within its granted authority an injected agent can still draft misleading recommendations; human review quality is the residual control.

history.change: Stale reference corrected: OWASP LLM Top 10 numbering updated to the 2026 edition; status unchanged

challenge.customer_intent: Use AI assistance without letting it move money, leak data or act outside the user's intent.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Indirect prompt injection causes an agent to submit, approve or export something harmful.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: The conventional answer, human-in-the-loop approval of agent output, degrades with volume and automation bias.
challenge.legally_required: No; sponsor fiduciary duties cannot be delegated to software (Sponsor Authority core boundary).
challenge.contractually_required: Emerging customer AI addenda ask for human oversight.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Agent approval of grants and live payments is eliminated in scope by withholding those command classes from every agent role in the deterministic authority matrix.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Tool broker and authorization core; intersection computed per call.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Agent action records with tools available, tier and delegation chain.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Deterministic capability withholding plus intersection semantics, with humans reviewing only what remains.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, by AUTH-T01 and AUTH-T08 style negative tests and inspection of the matrix.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely for read and draft uses; consequential agent actions will face skepticism regardless.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If any agent tool performs a consequential action without passing through the authorization core.
challenge.alternative_cost: Engineering of the broker and matrix.
challenge.alternative_risks: Users may over-trust agent drafts because the platform 'would have blocked anything dangerous'.
supporting_arguments: Aligns with OWASP LLM03:2026 excessive agency (LLM06 in the 2025 edition) mitigations.
opposing_arguments: Does not prevent harmful content within allowed actions.

title: Data-level authorization for exports, reporting, analytics and sensitive fields
status_rationale: The Sponsor Authority decision matrix classifies export of confidential partner evidence as A3/A4; UNB-XIN-IAM-003 requires step-up for data export; UNB-TEN-003 includes analytics paths in deny-by-default. Not implemented.
target_answer: Exports, scheduled reports and analytics are produced only through query handlers that apply the requester's scope and field-level permissions, never through direct database or warehouse access by users. Bulk exports require step-up, are logged with row counts and recipients, and above sponsor-set thresholds require a second approver. Sensitive fields (tax identifiers, bank details, dates of birth) are released only to roles that need them and are masked elsewhere. Any analytics store receives only data classes permitted by the isolation map and enforces the same tenant scope.
intended_practice: Implement export through governed handlers with field-level policy and approvals.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design applies the same authorization to exports and reports as to screens, requires step-up for bulk exports and restricts sensitive fields to roles that need them. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Once exported, data is outside platform control.
